title: Agent Architectures

techniques.name: Workflow Patterns
techniques.q: Do I need an agent at all?
techniques.what: Workflows run the model along code paths you wrote in advance; agents let the model choose its own steps and tools. The three core workflow patterns are prompt chaining (fixed steps with checks between them), routing (classify, then send each input down a specialised path) and parallelization (sectioning or voting). Start with the simplest pattern that works and add agentic freedom only when it measurably helps.
use: The steps can be written down before the task starts
Requests fall into a few known types, each with its own procedure
Audit, cost or latency limits call for predictable behaviour
metrics: a fixed sequence of calls, with plain-code gates between steps
a classifier sends each input to a specialised prompt or path
independent subtasks run at the same time, then join
the same check run several times or with several prompts; aggregate
low-confidence routes go to a general path or a human
the model picks the steps: more flexible, costlier, errors can compound
steps: Write the procedure down and mark which steps need a model at all
Put a plain-code check between steps so bad output stops early
Add a router only when request types need genuinely different handling
Measure accuracy, cost and unhandled cases before reaching for an agent
pitfalls: A router without a fallback silently misroutes unfamiliar requests
Rigid chains break on open-ended tasks nobody anticipated
Voting multiplies cost, so use it only where errors are expensive
techniques.remember: Write the path down if you can. Let the model steer only where you can’t.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: 1,000 health-insurance claims, one generic prompt against a router with specialised paths and a completeness gate.

cmp.best: Breaks on inputs nobody planned for

techniques.name: ReAct Loop
techniques.q: What should I do next, given what I just saw?
techniques.what: ReAct interleaves reasoning with actions: the model thinks, calls a tool, reads the observation and decides again, until it can answer. Because every step sees the latest result, it copes with paths nobody could predict. It is the default loop in most agent SDKs, and it needs a step cap, compact tool results and errors returned as observations.
use: The next step depends on what the last tool returned
Diagnosis and investigation tasks with branching paths
A small, well-described tool set the model can choose from reliably
metrics: the model reasons about what to do next
the tool’s result, appended to the history
a final answer, or a hard step cap
every call resends all earlier steps
returned to the model as observations, not raised as crashes
steps: Define a few tools with tight schemas and short, informative results
Run the loop: call the model, execute its tool calls, append the results, repeat
Cap the steps and stop gracefully with a partial answer
Log every trace so failures can be replayed and graded
pitfalls: No step cap means loops that never end
Verbose tool results inflate every later call
Re-deciding after every observation is slow and costly for routine tasks
techniques.remember: Think, act, observe. Cap the loop.
techniques.cap: Each call resends the whole history, so tokens grow with every step. Numbers are illustrative.

techniques.name: Plan-and-Execute
techniques.q: Can I plan the whole task before acting?
techniques.what: A planner writes the whole multi-step plan up front; executors, which can be smaller models or plain tool calls, run each step; a replanner steps in only when a step fails. ReWOO goes further: the plan names future results as variables (#E1, #E2), so tools run without a model call in between, and a solver writes the answer from the collected evidence.
use: Steps are knowable in advance, but deciding them one at a time is costly
Many tool calls that a small model or plain code can run
Latency matters and independent steps could run in parallel
metrics: planner writes steps, executor runs them, replan on failure
#E placeholders; no model call between tools; one solver call
the plan is a graph; independent calls run in parallel
“devise a plan, then carry it out” in a single prompt
a failed step, a surprising result or a budget breach
steps: Have the planner return a structured list of steps, not prose
Run each step with the cheapest executor that can do it
Store each result as evidence keyed by its step
Replan only when a step fails or the evidence contradicts the plan
pitfalls: A plan built on a wrong assumption fails late unless results are checked
Without replanning, one failed step sinks the whole task
Placeholders break when a tool returns an unexpected shape
techniques.remember: Plan once with the big model. Execute cheaply. Replan on failure.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: a 5-step airline rebooking as ReAct (a large-model call per step) against ReWOO (plan once, solve once).

cmp.best: A stale plan when the world changes

techniques.name: Reflection and Evaluator–Optimizer
techniques.q: Is this draft good enough, or should it go round again?
techniques.what: A generator drafts, an evaluator critiques the draft against clear criteria, and the generator revises until the draft passes or a round limit is hit. Self-Refine uses one model for every role; Reflexion keeps written lessons from failed attempts for the next try. The gains depend on feedback grounded in something outside the model: tests, rules or a checklist.
use: There is a clear standard to check against: tests, a rulebook, a schema
Drafts improve measurably with specific feedback
One or two extra rounds of latency are acceptable
metrics: one call drafts, another evaluates and gives feedback, in a loop
the same model drafts, critiques and revises
written lessons from failures are stored and reused on the next attempt
tests, validators, rule tables: the most reliable signal
pass, or a round cap; always keep the best draft
steps: Write the evaluation criteria first: tests, rules or a checklist
Turn each failure into a specific written critique
Revise with the critique, then evaluate again
Cap the rounds and return the best-scoring draft, not the last one
pitfalls: Self-critique with no external signal can make answers worse
Unbounded loops burn tokens on marginal gains
Returning the last draft instead of the best one ships regressions
techniques.remember: Critique against something real. Keep the best draft.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: a draft checked against 10 rules; each critique lists only the rules that failed.

techniques.name: Search-Based Reasoning
techniques.q: Should I try several paths before committing?
techniques.what: Instead of committing to one line of reasoning, the model proposes several candidate thoughts at each step, a value function scores them, and a search (breadth-first, depth-first or Monte Carlo tree search) expands the promising ones and backs out of dead ends. Tree of Thoughts applies this to reasoning; LATS adds tool actions, environment feedback and reflection.
use: Early wrong choices commit you and are costly to undo
There is a reliable way to score partial solutions
Accuracy matters more than cost or latency
metrics: candidate thoughts generated from each state
how many top candidates survive each level
how many steps deep the search goes
scores a state: sure, likely or impossible, or a number
BFS, DFS with backtracking, or MCTS with UCT
the cheapest cousin: sample several chains and take a majority vote
steps: Define a thought: one step small enough to evaluate on its own
Write a value prompt or check that can prune impossible states
Start small, such as k = 3 and b = 2, with a depth that fits the problem
Count model calls per solved task and compare with a single chain
pitfalls: Calls multiply with k, b and d, so costs rise fast
A noisy value function prunes good branches and keeps bad ones
Overkill for tasks a single chain already solves
techniques.remember: Branch when mistakes commit you. Prune with a good judge.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: 3 proposals per state, the best 2 kept; branches scored as impossible are pruned.

techniques.name: Reasoning Models and Thinking Budgets
techniques.q: How much should the model think before answering?
techniques.what: Reasoning models are trained, largely with reinforcement learning, to think at length before they answer. You control that test-time compute with a thinking budget or an effort level. More thinking helps on hard problems and wastes money and time on easy ones, so the budget should follow difficulty.
use: The difficulty sits inside one hard problem: maths, code, multi-constraint decisions
Mixed traffic where a router can separate easy from hard
Planner or judge steps, where one better call saves many later ones
metrics: budget_tokens ≥ 1,024 and below max_tokens, on models that support it
thinking type “adaptive”; output_config.effort sets how much
reasoning.effort, with model-dependent values such as low, medium, high
thinking and reasoning tokens are billed as output tokens
reasoning tokens occupy the context window and the output limit
low effort for routine cases, high for hard ones
steps: Measure accuracy and cost with no or low thinking first
Raise the budget on the hard slice and watch where the gains flatten
Route by difficulty so easy requests stay cheap
Log thinking tokens from usage and leave headroom in the output limit
pitfalls: A flat maximum budget pays for thinking on easy requests
An output limit that is too small truncates the answer or rejects the request
More thinking does not fix missing information or missing tools
techniques.remember: Spend thinking where the problem is hard, not everywhere.
techniques.cap: Illustrative numbers for a fictional model, Gamma-R. Hard-case accuracy flattens while tokens keep rising.

cmp.best: Paying to think on easy work

techniques.name: Human-in-the-Loop Checkpoints
techniques.q: Should a person approve this before it happens?
techniques.what: The agent works on its own until it reaches an action that is risky, irreversible or above a limit, and then pauses. Its state is saved, a person approves, edits or rejects the proposed action, and the run resumes from exactly where it stopped, even hours later. Frameworks call the pause an interrupt or an approval; the design work is choosing which steps pause and what the reviewer sees.
use: Actions that move money, change records or contact customers
Steps above a policy limit, such as refunds over ₹10,000
Early rollout, while you still measure how often the agent is wrong
metrics: a pause point before a tool call or inside a step, chosen by a rule
always, never, or a function of the arguments, such as amount or customer type
the paused run is stored (a checkpointer or serialised run state) so it can wait hours
what the reviewer sees: the action, its arguments, the reason and the evidence
approve, edit the arguments, or reject with a note the agent reads
continue from the saved point with the decision, and log who decided
steps: List the actions and mark which are irreversible or above a limit
Put the approval rule in code on the tool or step, not in the prompt
Save the paused run durably and send the reviewer a short card with the evidence
Resume with the decision, and log who approved what and when
pitfalls: Pausing on every step trains reviewers to approve without reading
Side effects placed before the pause run again when the step restarts
A paused run kept only in memory is lost on the next deploy or restart
techniques.remember: Pause before what you cannot undo. Save the state, show the evidence, resume cleanly.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: 1,000 refund requests a day at KhataPay, a fictional wallet, with a ₹10,000 approval limit.

cmp.scope: Your code pauses; a person decides
cmp.needs: Medium: saved state and a review screen

techniques.name: Code as Action (CodeAct)
techniques.q: Should the agent write code instead of calling tools one at a time?
techniques.what: The agent’s action is a short program rather than a single tool call. Tools are exposed as functions, and the model writes code with loops, variables and conditions that calls them, runs it in a sandbox and reads the output. Multi-step data work takes far fewer turns and tokens, but running model-written code needs isolation: no network by default, only allow-listed tools and libraries, time and memory limits, and review of anything that writes.
use: Bulk or repetitive work: reconciling hundreds of records, transforming files
Calculations and data analysis the model should not do in its head
Chaining several tools where each output feeds the next
metrics: the model calls typed Python functions, not JSON one at a time
a container or micro-VM with no network by default
only named tools and imports are available
CPU time, memory, output size and number of turns
stdout, errors and return values go back to the model
writes and payments still pass policy checks or a person
steps: Expose tools as typed functions with docstrings
Run the model’s code in a sandbox with no network, allow-listed tools and limits
Return output and errors so the model can fix and retry
Keep writes behind the same policy checks as normal tool calls
pitfalls: Running generated code on the host with network access
Letting code import anything, including shell and HTTP libraries
Assuming code actions are safe because the model wrote them
techniques.remember: Let it write code, but run the code in a box.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: Bazaarkart, a fictional marketplace, reconciles 200 orders across three tools.

import json
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()
SMALL, LARGE = "claude-haiku-4-5", "claude-sonnet-4-5"   # use current models

def ask(model, prompt, max_tokens=600):
    r = client.messages.create(model=model, max_tokens=max_tokens,
                               messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}])
    return r.content[0].text

def extract(email):                                                   #@1
    prompt = "Extract policy_no, amount, hospital as JSON:\n" + email    #@1
    return json.loads(ask(SMALL, prompt))                              #@1

def complete(f):                                                      #@2
    return bool(f.get("policy_no")) and f.get("amount", 0) > 0        #@2

def route(email):                                                     #@3
    out = json.loads(ask(SMALL, ROUTER_PROMPT + email, 60))           #@3
    if out["confidence"] < 0.7:                                        #@4
        return "general"                        # or a human queue     #@4
    return out["route"]            # cashless | reimbursement | other  #@3

def vote(fields):                                                     #@6
    flags = [ask(SMALL, p + json.dumps(fields), 20) for p in FRAUD_PROMPTS]  #@6
    return sum(f.strip() == "SUSPECT" for f in flags) >= 2            #@6

def handle(email):
    fields = extract(email)                                           #@1
    if not complete(fields):                                          #@2
        return {"status": "sent back for documents"}                  #@2
    path = route(email)                                               #@3,4
    with ThreadPoolExecutor() as pool:                                #@5
        fraud = pool.submit(vote, fields)                             #@5,6
        summary = pool.submit(ask, LARGE, PATHS[path] + json.dumps(fields))  #@1,5
    return {"route": path, "summary": summary.result(), "suspect": fraud.result()}  #@5
steps: Chain fixed steps
The claim email goes through a fixed sequence: a small model extracts the fields, then a path prompt writes the summary. Your code, not the model, decides the order.
Gate between steps
A plain-code check sits between the steps. A claim with no policy number or amount is sent back for documents instead of producing a confident but wrong summary.
Route by request type
A cheap classifier sends each claim down a specialised path: cashless 55%, reimbursement 30%, other 15%. Each path has its own prompt and checks.
Fall back when unsure
If the router's confidence is below 0.7, the claim goes to a general path or a human queue. Without this, unfamiliar requests are silently misrouted.
Section: run independent parts together
The fraud screen and the summary do not depend on each other, so they run at the same time. The slower one sets the latency: 4.1 s instead of 7.8 s one after the other.
Vote where errors are expensive
Three independent fraud prompts review the claim and it is flagged when two agree. Voting triples the cost of that check, so keep it for decisions where a miss is costly.

import anthropic
client = anthropic.Anthropic()

TOOLS = [                                                          #@1
    {"name": "get_order", "description": "Order status by order id",  #@1
     "input_schema": {"type": "object",                              #@1
                      "properties": {"order_id": {"type": "string"}},  #@1
                      "required": ["order_id"]}},                    #@1
    # get_courier_status and raise_ticket are defined the same way
]
MAX_STEPS = 8                                                       #@5

def run(question):
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": question}]
    for step in range(MAX_STEPS):                                   #@4,5
        r = client.messages.create(model="claude-sonnet-4-5", max_tokens=1024,
                                   tools=TOOLS, messages=messages)   #@2,4
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": r.content})  #@2
        if r.stop_reason != "tool_use":                              #@5
            return r.content[-1].text                                #@5
        results = []
        for call in [b for b in r.content if b.type == "tool_use"]:  #@3
            try:
                out = TOOL_FNS[call.name](**call.input)              #@3
            except Exception as e:                                   #@6
                out = f"error: {e}"         # an observation, not a crash  #@6
            results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": call.id,
                            "content": out[:1500]})                  #@3
        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})        #@3,4
    return "Stopped at the step cap; handing over to a human."       #@5
steps: Define a few tight tools
Three tools with short descriptions and strict input schemas. The model can only act through them, so clear names and required fields matter more than clever prompts.
Think, then act
The model reads the question and replies with a tool call rather than an answer: get_order for order 8812. The stop reason tool_use tells your loop to run it.
Observe the result
Your code runs the tool and appends the result as a tool_result message: “shipped”. That observation is what the next step reasons about.
Loop with the growing history
The model is called again with everything so far and asks for the courier status: “held at hub”. Each call resends the whole history, so input grows from 1.2k to 3.4k to 5.8k tokens.
Stop on an answer or the cap
On the third call the model answers instead of calling a tool, so the loop ends after 3 of the 8 allowed steps. If the cap is reached first, the loop stops and hands over.
Return errors as observations
When the courier API times out, the loop returns “error: timeout” as the tool result. The model retries or picks another route instead of the whole run crashing.

import re
from typing import TypedDict
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END
# planner and solver: a large chat model; planner uses structured output

class S(TypedDict):
    task: str
    steps: list      # [(var, tool, arg)], e.g. ("#E2", "find_flights", "#E1")
    evidence: dict   # {"#E1": "PNR 6XK2QT, DEL-BOM, AI-865 cancelled"}
    failed: bool
    answer: str

def plan(s):                                                         #@1
    out = planner.invoke(PLAN_PROMPT.format(task=s["task"], done=s["evidence"]))  #@1,4
    return {"steps": out.steps, "failed": False}                     #@1

def execute(s):                                                      #@2
    var, tool, arg = next(x for x in s["steps"] if x[0] not in s["evidence"])  #@2
    arg = re.sub(r"#E\d+", lambda m: s["evidence"][m.group()], arg)   #@5
    ok, out = TOOLS[tool](arg)                  # no model call here  #@2,5
    if not ok:
        return {"failed": True}                                      #@4
    return {"evidence": {**s["evidence"], var: out}}                  #@3

def solve(s):                                                        #@6
    msg = solver.invoke(SOLVE_PROMPT.format(task=s["task"], ev=s["evidence"]))  #@6
    return {"answer": msg.content}                                   #@6

def after_execute(s):                                                #@4
    if s["failed"]:
        return "plan"                              # replan on failure  #@4
    todo = [v for v, _, _ in s["steps"] if v not in s["evidence"]]     #@3
    return "execute" if todo else "solve"                            #@3

g = StateGraph(S)
g.add_node("plan", plan); g.add_node("execute", execute); g.add_node("solve", solve)
g.add_edge(START, "plan"); g.add_edge("plan", "execute")             #@1,2
g.add_conditional_edges("execute", after_execute, ["plan", "execute", "solve"])  #@4
g.add_edge("solve", END)                                             #@6
app = g.compile()
steps: Plan the whole task once
One large-model call writes a structured plan: four tool steps, each with a variable name. #E2 needs #E1, #E3 needs #E2, and so on.
Execute with the cheapest executor
The executor node takes the next unfinished step and runs it. Here it is a plain tool call; in plan-and-execute it can be a small model.
Record evidence by step
Each result is stored under its variable: #E1 is the PNR, #E2 the replacement flight. The router edge keeps executing until every step has evidence.
Replan only on failure
The seat hold for #E3 fails because the seat has gone. The conditional edge sends the state back to the planner with the evidence so far, and only then is the large model called again.
ReWOO: fill placeholders, not prompts
Before a tool runs, #E1 in its input is replaced with the stored value. No model reads the observation in between, which is where ReWOO saves most of its tokens.
Solve once at the end
A single solver call reads the task and all the evidence and writes the passenger's answer. Two large calls in total when nothing fails, three with one replan.

import subprocess, anthropic
client = anthropic.Anthropic()

def ask(prompt):
    r = client.messages.create(model="claude-sonnet-4-5", max_tokens=2000,
                               messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}])
    return r.content[0].text

def run_tests(code):                                                   #@2
    open("emi.py", "w").write(code)                                      #@2
    p = subprocess.run(["pytest", "-q", "test_emi.py"],                  #@2
                       capture_output=True, text=True)                   #@2
    failed = [l for l in p.stdout.splitlines() if l.startswith("FAILED")]  #@2,3
    return p.returncode == 0, failed                                   #@2

lessons = []                            # kept across tasks (Reflexion)  #@5

def solve(spec, max_rounds=4):
    code = ask(spec + "\nLessons from earlier tasks: " + "; ".join(lessons))  #@1,5
    best, best_fails = code, None                                      #@6
    for r in range(max_rounds):                                        #@6
        ok, failed = run_tests(code)                                   #@2
        if best_fails is None or len(failed) < best_fails:             #@6
            best, best_fails = code, len(failed)                       #@6
        if ok:
            return code                                                #@6
        critique = "These tests fail:\n" + "\n".join(failed)            #@3
        if r < max_rounds - 1:
            code = ask(f"{spec}\n\nCode:\n{code}\n\n{critique}\nFix the code.")  #@4
    lessons.append(ask("One-line lesson from these failures:\n" + critique))  #@5
    return best                                                        #@6
steps: Generate a first draft
The model writes an EMI calculator from the spec. Nothing is checked yet, so this is only a candidate.
Evaluate against something real
pytest runs 10 tests on the draft. 6 pass and 4 fail. The feedback comes from outside the model, which is what makes the loop reliable.
Turn failures into a critique
The failing test names and messages become a short, specific critique, such as test_zero_rate: ZeroDivisionError, instead of “please improve”.
Revise with the critique
The model rewrites the code with the critique in view. Version 2 passes 9 of 10, and the loop goes round again.
Remember lessons across tasks
When a task ends with failures, a one-line lesson is saved and added to the next task's prompt. That is Reflexion's idea: learn from the attempt, not just revise within it.
Cap the rounds and keep the best
Version 3 passes all 10 tests, so the loop stops at round 3 of 4. Had it hit the cap, it would return the best-scoring version, not the last one.

import math

def propose(route, k):                                               #@1
    out = ask(f"Stops so far: {route}\nSuggest {k} possible next stops, one per line.")  #@1
    return out.splitlines()[:k]                                      #@1

def value(route):                                                    #@2
    v = ask(f"Route: {route}\nCan every time window still be met? "  #@2
            "Answer sure, likely or impossible.").strip().lower()     #@2
    return {"sure": 20, "likely": 1, "impossible": 0.001}.get(v, 0.001)  #@2

def tot_bfs(start, k=3, b=2, depth=3):
    frontier = [[start]]
    for _ in range(depth):                                           #@4
        cands = [r + [s] for r in frontier for s in propose(r, k)]   #@1,4
        scored = [(value(c), c) for c in cands]                      #@2
        scored = [x for x in scored if x[1] and x[0] > 0.001]  # prune  #@5
        scored.sort(key=lambda x: x[0], reverse=True)                #@3
        frontier = [c for _, c in scored[:b]]                        #@3
        if not frontier:
            return None                                              #@5
    return frontier[0]                                               #@4

def uct(child, parent_visits, c=1.4):                                 #@6
    if child.visits == 0:
        return float("inf")                     # try unvisited first  #@6
    exploit = child.value / child.visits                             #@6
    explore = c * math.sqrt(math.log(parent_visits) / child.visits)  #@6
    return exploit + explore                                         #@6
steps: Propose k candidate thoughts
From the depot, the model proposes k = 3 possible first stops: the hospital, the pharmacy or the cold-chain drop. Each is one small, checkable step.
Evaluate each candidate
A value prompt rates each partial route as sure, likely or impossible, mapped to 20, 1 and 0.001 as in the Tree of Thoughts code. Pharmacy first is impossible: it opens after the hospital's deadline.
Select the best b
Only the top b = 2 candidates survive: hospital first (sure) and cold-chain first (likely). The impossible branch is dropped, so no more calls are spent on it.
Expand level by level
Each kept route gets 3 new proposals, so the second level has 6 candidates. The search repeats propose, evaluate and select until the depth limit.
Prune dead ends
Two of the six second-level routes break a time window and are pruned. The surviving branch from the hospital reaches a valid route at depth 3.
MCTS variant: balance value and exploration
Monte Carlo tree search, as in LATS, picks which node to expand with UCT: average value plus an exploration bonus that is largest for rarely visited nodes. Unvisited nodes go first.

import anthropic
from openai import OpenAI
claude, oai = anthropic.Anthropic(), OpenAI()
MODEL = "claude-sonnet-4-5"       # a model that supports manual budgets

def baseline(case):                                                  #@1
    return claude.messages.create(model=MODEL, max_tokens=1500,       #@1
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": case}])                #@1

def think(case, budget):                                             #@2
    assert 1024 <= budget < 20000       # at least 1,024, below max_tokens  #@3
    return claude.messages.create(model=MODEL, max_tokens=20000,      #@2,3
        thinking={"type": "enabled", "budget_tokens": budget},       #@2
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": case}])                #@2

def review(case, hard):                                              #@5
    r = think(case, 16000) if hard else baseline(case)               #@5
    log(output_tokens=r.usage.output_tokens)   # includes thinking     #@4
    return next(b.text for b in r.content if b.type == "text")       #@2

def review_openai(case, hard):                                       #@5
    r = oai.responses.create(model="o4-mini", input=case,            #@5
        reasoning={"effort": "high" if hard else "low"})             #@5
    log(reasoning=r.usage.output_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens)    #@4
    return r.output_text

def agent_step(messages):                                            #@6
    return claude.beta.messages.create(model=MODEL, max_tokens=16000,  #@6
        betas=["interleaved-thinking-2025-05-14"], tools=TOOLS,       #@6
        thinking={"type": "enabled", "budget_tokens": 10000},        #@6
        messages=messages)       # keep thinking blocks in the history  #@6
steps: Measure a baseline without thinking
Run the underwriting cases with no thinking first. Easy top-ups are already 96% correct; hard thin-file cases only 41%. That gap is what a budget should close.
Enable thinking with a budget
Pass thinking with type enabled and a budget_tokens value. At a 4,000-token budget, hard-case accuracy rises to 74%. The response now contains thinking blocks before the text.
Respect the limits
The manual budget must be at least 1,024 tokens and below max_tokens, because thinking counts towards the output limit. Leave room for the answer itself.
Measure thinking in the usage
Thinking tokens are billed as output. A hard case at a 16k budget used about 14,400 thinking tokens plus a 350-token answer, so log output tokens per request.
Route by difficulty
Easy cases go without thinking and hard ones get 16k. With 80% easy traffic, average output falls from 6,430 tokens (16k for everyone) to 3,230. OpenAI's reasoning.effort works the same way.
Interleave thinking with tool calls
In agent loops, interleaved thinking lets the model think again after each tool result. On Claude 4 models in manual mode it needs a beta header, and thinking blocks must stay in the history.

from typing import TypedDict
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END
from langgraph.types import interrupt, Command
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import InMemorySaver   # use Postgres in production  #@3

LIMIT = 10_000   # rupees: the rule lives in code, not in the prompt   #@1

class S(TypedDict, total=False):
    ticket: str; plan: dict; note: str

def decide(state):                                                      #@2
    return {"plan": propose_refund(state["ticket"])}   # propose, don't act  #@2

def approve(state):
    plan = state["plan"]
    if plan["amount"] <= LIMIT:                                         #@1
        return Command(goto="pay")
    decision = interrupt({"action": "refund", "amount": plan["amount"],  #@3,4
                          "reason": plan["reason"], "evidence": plan["evidence"]})  #@4
    if decision["verdict"] == "reject":                                 #@5
        return Command(goto="explain", update={"note": decision["note"]})  #@5
    if decision["verdict"] == "edit":                                   #@5
        plan = {**plan, "amount": decision["amount"]}                   #@5
    return Command(goto="pay", update={"plan": plan})                   #@5

def pay(state):
    issue_refund(state["plan"], idempotency_key=state["ticket"])        #@6
    return {}

g = StateGraph(S)
for name, fn in [("decide", decide), ("approve", approve), ("pay", pay), ("explain", explain)]:
    g.add_node(name, fn)
g.add_edge(START, "decide"); g.add_edge("decide", "approve")
g.add_edge("pay", END); g.add_edge("explain", END)
app = g.compile(checkpointer=InMemorySaver())                           #@3
cfg = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "T-7731"}}                         #@3

out = app.invoke({"ticket": "T-7731"}, cfg)   # returns with out["__interrupt__"]  #@4
# ...hours later, from the review screen:
app.invoke(Command(resume={"verdict": "approve"}), cfg)                 #@5
steps: Put the rule in code

The approval limit is a constant in code: ₹10,000. Refunds at or below it go straight to payment. The prompt never decides whether a person is needed, so a clever customer message cannot talk its way past the check.
Propose, don't act
The decide step only proposes: refund ₹25,000 on ticket T-7731, with a reason and the evidence it used. Proposing and acting are separate steps, so a check can sit between them.
Pause and save the state
The amount is above the limit, so interrupt() pauses the run. The checkpointer saves the whole state under the thread id T-7731, and invoke returns at once. Nothing waits in memory.
Show the reviewer the evidence

The value passed to interrupt() is what the caller receives in __interrupt__: the action, amount, reason and evidence. Your review screen turns it into a card, so the reviewer judges facts, not a bare yes or no.
Resume with the decision

Hours later the reviewer approves, edits the amount or rejects with a note. Command(resume=…) continues the same thread, and the decision becomes the return value of interrupt(). The approve step restarts from its first line, so nothing before the pause may have side effects.
Act once, after approval
Only the pay step touches money, and it runs after the decision. The idempotency key tied to the ticket means a retried payment call cannot refund twice.

from smolagents import CodeAgent, tool, InferenceClientModel

@tool                                                                   #@1
def payment(order_id: str) -> dict:                                     #@1
    """Payment status for an order. Args: order_id: the order id."""    #@1
    return payments_api.get(order_id)

@tool
def courier(awb: str) -> dict:
    """Delivery status for an air waybill. Args: awb: the waybill number."""
    return courier_api.track(awb)

agent = CodeAgent(
    tools=[payment, courier, list_orders, flag_order],                  #@1
    model=InferenceClientModel(),
    additional_authorized_imports=["datetime"],       # nothing else   #@3
    executor_type="e2b",                   # remote sandbox, not the host   #@2
    max_steps=8,                                                        #@4
)
result = agent.run("Reconcile yesterday's orders: flag any where payment "   #@5
                   "and courier status disagree. Do not refund anything.")   #@5,6
# The model writes and runs code such as:
#   for o in list_orders(date="2026-09-26"):
#       if payment(o["id"])["status"] != courier(o["awb"])["status"]:
#           flag_order(o["id"])
steps: Expose tools as typed functions
Each tool is a Python function with a docstring and types. The model can call them inside its own code, in loops and conditions.
Run the code in a sandbox
The code runs in a remote sandbox, not on your server. By default it has no network and no access to your files or secrets.
Allow-list what code may import
Only named imports are permitted. A program that tries to import requests or subprocess fails before it runs.
Cap steps and time
At most 8 turns, with limits on CPU time and output. A runaway loop stops instead of burning tokens.
Read output, fix, retry
Printed results and errors go back to the model, which can correct its code in the next turn. Here the whole reconciliation takes 6 turns.
Keep writes behind checks
flag_order only marks orders for a person. Refunds and other writes still pass the same policy checks as any tool call.

import json
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()
SMALL, LARGE = "claude-haiku-4-5", "claude-sonnet-4-5"   # use your current models
PATHS = {"cashless": "Check pre-authorisation fields...",
         "reimbursement": "Check bills, discharge summary...",
         "general": "Answer the policyholder's question..."}

def ask(model, prompt, max_tokens=800):
    r = client.messages.create(model=model, max_tokens=max_tokens,
                               messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}])
    return r.content[0].text

def route(email):                                   # routing
    out = json.loads(ask(SMALL, 'Classify as cashless, reimbursement or general. '
                                'Reply as JSON {"route": ..., "confidence": 0-1}\n' + email, 100))
    return out["route"] if out["confidence"] >= 0.7 else "general"   # fallback

def handle(email):
    path = route(email)
    fields = json.loads(ask(SMALL, "Extract policy_no, amount, hospital as JSON:\n" + email))
    if not fields.get("policy_no"):                 # gate between chain steps
        return {"status": "sent back", "reason": "policy number missing"}
    with ThreadPoolExecutor() as pool:              # sectioning: run in parallel
        fraud = pool.submit(ask, SMALL, "List fraud red flags:\n" + json.dumps(fields))
        summary = pool.submit(ask, LARGE, PATHS[path] + "\n" + json.dumps(fields))
    return {"route": path, "summary": summary.result(), "flags": fraud.result()}

from typing import TypedDict
from pydantic import BaseModel
from langchain_anthropic import ChatAnthropic
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END

class Plan(BaseModel):
    steps: list[str]              # e.g. "find_flights: DEL-BOM tomorrow"

class State(TypedDict):
    task: str
    plan: list[str]
    done: list[tuple[str, str]]   # (step, result)
    failed: bool

planner = ChatAnthropic(model="claude-sonnet-4-5").with_structured_output(Plan)

def plan(s: State):
    p = planner.invoke(f"Task: {s['task']}\nCompleted: {s['done']}\n"
                       "Write the remaining steps as 'tool: input'.")
    return {"plan": p.steps, "failed": False}

def execute(s: State):
    step = s["plan"][0]
    tool, arg = step.split(":", 1)
    ok, result = TOOLS[tool.strip()](arg.strip())      # plain tool call, no LLM
    if not ok:
        return {"failed": True}
    return {"plan": s["plan"][1:], "done": s["done"] + [(step, result)]}

def next_node(s: State):
    if s["failed"]:
        return "plan"                                   # replan only on failure
    return "execute" if s["plan"] else END

g = StateGraph(State)
g.add_node("plan", plan)
g.add_node("execute", execute)
g.add_edge(START, "plan")
g.add_edge("plan", "execute")
g.add_conditional_edges("execute", next_node, ["plan", "execute", END])
app = g.compile()
out = app.invoke({"task": "Rebook PNR 6XK2QT after AI-865 cancellation",
                  "plan": [], "done": [], "failed": False})
planexec.note: TOOLS stands for your own tool functions. Structured output keeps the plan machine-readable.

def bfs(start, k=3, b=2, depth=4):
    frontier = [start]                                   # partial routes
    calls = 0
    for _ in range(depth):
        candidates = []
        for state in frontier:
            for nxt in propose(state, k):                # k thoughts per state
                calls += 1
                candidates.append((value(state + [nxt]), state + [nxt]))
        candidates = [c for c in candidates if c[0] > 0]  # prune impossible
        candidates.sort(key=lambda c: c[0], reverse=True)
        frontier = [route for _, route in candidates[:b]] # keep the beam
        if not frontier:
            return None, calls
    return frontier[0], calls

import asyncio
from agents import Agent, Runner, function_tool

async def over_limit(_ctx, params, _call_id) -> bool:
    return params["amount"] > 10_000          # the rule lives in code

@function_tool(needs_approval=over_limit)
async def issue_refund(ticket_id: str, amount: int) -> str:
    """Refund a customer to the original payment method."""
    return f"refunded ₹{amount} for {ticket_id}"

agent = Agent(name="Refunds",
              instructions="Resolve refund tickets. Check the facts, then use issue_refund.",
              tools=[issue_refund])

async def main():
    result = await Runner.run(agent, "Ticket T-7731: rent of ₹25,000 was debited twice.")
    if result.interruptions:                   # paused before the refund ran
        state = result.to_state()
        for item in result.interruptions:
            print("Needs approval:", item.name, item.arguments)
            state.approve(item)                # or state.reject(item)
        result = await Runner.run(agent, state)
    print(result.final_output)

asyncio.run(main())

workflows.title: Router with a confidence fallback
workflows.explain: The comparison is inverted. It sends every confident prediction to the general path and keeps the unsure ones on specialised paths, the opposite of a fallback. Cost rises and misroutes stay.

also.3: Correct: the router first picks the most probable path.
also.5: Correct: a low-confidence claim should go to the general path or a human.

react.title: Returning tool results to the model
react.code:
for call in tool_calls:
    out = TOOL_FNS[call.name](**call.input)
    results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": call.id,
                    "content": json.dumps(call.input)})
messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})
react.explain: The tool message carries the call’s arguments instead of its result, so the model never sees the observation. It keeps asking for the same lookup until the step cap stops it.

also.2: Correct: the tool runs with the arguments the model chose.
also.5: Correct: tool results go back to the model in a user message.

planexec.title: Replanning in a plan-and-execute loop
planexec.explain: The condition is inverted: the loop replans after the first success and never records its result, while a failed step falls through and stores a bad value as evidence. Replanning belongs to failures only.

also.4: Correct: the replanner gets the evidence so far and the step that failed.
also.6: Correct: a successful result is stored under the step’s variable, such as #E2.

reflect.title: Keeping the best draft in a revision loop
reflect.code:
best, best_score = draft, evaluate(draft)
for r in range(max_rounds):
    draft = revise(draft, critique(draft))
    score = evaluate(draft)
    if score > best_score:
        best, best_score = draft, score
    if score == MAX_SCORE: break
return draft
reflect.explain: The loop tracks the best draft and then ignores it. If the last revision scored lower than an earlier one, the regression is what gets shipped.

also.1: Correct: the first draft is scored so later drafts have something to beat.
also.7: Correct: stop early once every check passes.

search.title: UCT score for choosing a node to expand
search.explain: Subtracting the exploration term penalises the nodes that have been tried least, so the search keeps expanding the same branch and never explores. UCT adds the bonus.

also.4: Correct: unvisited children get infinite priority, so each is tried once.
also.6: Correct: the bonus shrinks as a child is visited more often.

reasoning.title: Enabling a thinking budget
reasoning.code:
r = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-5",
    max_tokens=2000,
    thinking={"type": "enabled", "budget_tokens": 4000},
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": case}],
)
reasoning.explain: Thinking counts towards the output limit, so a manual budget_tokens must be below max_tokens (interleaved thinking is the exception). With 2,000 against 4,000 the request is rejected. Raise max_tokens above the budget with room for the answer.

also.2: Correct: a model that supports manual thinking budgets.
also.4: 4,000 is a valid budget: it is at least 1,024. The problem is the limit it has to fit under.

hitl.title: Notifying before the approval
hitl.fix: # send the SMS in the pay step, after the decision
hitl.explain: The SMS promises a refund before anyone has approved it, and because the step restarts from its first line on resume, the customer gets the message twice. Anything before interrupt() must be safe to repeat; notifications belong after the decision.

also.4: Correct: the pause carries the action and amount the reviewer needs.
also.6: Correct: the decision comes back as the value of interrupt().

codeact.title: Running the agent’s code
codeact.explain: exec runs model-written code in the app process, with the server’s network, files and credentials, and the default builtins allow any import. One injected instruction can read secrets or send data out. Run the code in an isolated sandbox instead.

also.2: Exposing only named tools is the right idea, but exec still grants everything else.
also.4: Capturing stdout for the model is fine.

2: The extracted fields have no policy number. What should happen next?
Stop in code and send the claim back for documents
Let the summary step work around the missing field
A plain-code gate is cheap and certain. Letting a model guess past missing data produces confident, wrong summaries.
3: Claims come in three kinds with different procedures. What decides the path?
The large model reads each claim and improvises a procedure
A cheap classifier routes each claim to a specialised path
Routing is a workflow pattern: a small, cheap call picks the path, and each path has its own prompt and checks.
4: The router is only 55% sure about a claim. What should it do?
Send it to the most likely path anyway
Send it to a general path or a human queue
Below the confidence threshold, fall back. Otherwise unfamiliar requests are silently misrouted.
5: The fraud screen takes 3.7 s and the summary 4.1 s, and neither needs the other. What is the total latency if they run together?
About 4.1 s
About 7.8 s
Sectioning runs independent parts in parallel, so the slower part sets the latency: 4.1 s, not 3.7 + 4.1.
6: Three fraud prompts return SUSPECT, SUSPECT and clear. What does the vote decide?
Flag the claim: two of three agree
Clear it: the checks disagree
Voting aggregates independent checks; a majority of two out of three flags the claim for review.

2: The model has the question and the tools. What does it return first?
A final answer from its own knowledge
A tool call: get_order for order 8812
In a ReAct loop the model acts when it needs information; the stop reason tool_use tells the loop to run the tool.
3: The tool returns “shipped”. Where does that go?
Into a tool_result message appended to the history
Into a log file only
The observation must go back to the model, or the next step reasons without it.
4: The model is called again. What does this call send?
Only the latest observation
The whole history: question, calls and results so far
Models are stateless, so each call resends everything. That is why input grows from 1.2k to 3.4k to 5.8k tokens.
5: The model now returns text with no tool call. What does the loop do?
Stop and return the answer
Keep looping until the cap of 8
No tool call means the model has finished. The cap is a safety limit, not a target.
6: The courier API throws a timeout. What should the loop do?
Let the exception end the run
Return “error: timeout” to the model as the tool result
An error is an observation the model can act on: retry, try another tool, or explain the delay.

2: The plan has four steps. What runs step #E1?
The executor: a tool call or a small model
The large planner, one step at a time
The planner only plans. Cheap executors or plain tools run the steps, which is where the savings come from.
3: get_pnr returns the booking. Where is it kept?
In the model's context only
In state, under its variable #E1
Evidence is stored by step, so later steps and the solver can use it without re-reading the whole history.
4: hold_seat for #E3 fails: the seat is gone. What happens?
The run continues to #E4 anyway
The graph routes back to the planner with the evidence so far
Replanning is triggered by failure. The planner sees what is done and writes a new route from step 3.
5: find_flights needs the PNR from #E1. How does it get it?
The placeholder #E1 is replaced with the stored value, with no model call
A model reads the evidence and writes the tool input
That substitution is ReWOO's key idea: tools chain through variables, so no model call sits between them.
6: All evidence is collected. How many more large-model calls are needed?
One solver call
One per step, to summarise each result
A single solver call reads the task and evidence and writes the answer: two large calls in total without failures.

2: The draft exists. What should judge it?
Something external: 10 unit tests
The same model, asked if the draft looks right
External feedback is reliable. Self-assessment alone can miss errors or even make answers worse.
3: Four tests fail. What goes back to the model?
The failing test names and error messages
A general instruction to improve the code
Specific failures tell the model exactly what to fix. Vague critique gives vague revisions.
4: The model revises with the critique. What is likely next?
Every test passes on the first revision
More tests pass, but the loop may need another round
Revisions usually help step by step: here 6 → 9 of 10, so the loop goes round again.
5: The task ended with failures. What does Reflexion keep for next time?
The full failed code
A short written lesson, added to the next task's prompt
Reflexion stores verbal lessons from failures in memory, so later attempts start better.
6: The cap is reached and round 4 scored lower than round 3. What should the loop return?
The round 3 draft: the best score
The round 4 draft: the latest
Always return the best-scoring draft. The last revision can be a regression.

2: Three first stops are proposed. What decides which to explore?
A value prompt rates each partial route
The model's favourite is always expanded first
Tree of Thoughts scores each candidate state, for example sure, likely or impossible, before choosing.
3: Scores are sure, impossible and likely, with a beam of 2. Which survive?
All three, to be safe
Sure and likely
The beam keeps the top b candidates. The impossible branch gets no more calls.
4: Each of the 2 kept routes gets 3 proposals. How many candidates at level 2?
b × k = 2 × 3 = 6 candidates, each generated and evaluated.
5: Two level-2 routes break a time window. What happens to them?
They are kept in case the evaluator is wrong
They are pruned and never expanded
Pruning impossible states is what keeps the search affordable.
6: In MCTS, a child has never been visited. What is its UCT score?
Zero, because it has no value yet
Infinite, so it is tried first
Unvisited children get top priority; after that, the exploration bonus shrinks as visits grow.

2: You enable thinking with a 4,000-token budget. What happens to hard-case accuracy?
It rises, here from 41% to 74%
It stays the same; only latency changes
Thinking helps most on hard, multi-step problems. On easy cases it adds little.
3: You set budget_tokens to 16,000. What must max_tokens be?
Anything; they are independent
Above 16,000, with room for the answer
Thinking counts towards the output limit, so the manual budget must sit below max_tokens.
4: How are thinking tokens billed?
As output tokens
Free: only the answer is billed
Thinking tokens are billed as output, so they dominate the cost of hard answers.
5: 80% of files are easy. What cuts cost most without hurting hard cases?
Lower the budget for everyone
Route easy files to no thinking and keep 16k for hard ones
Routing by difficulty keeps easy files cheap: average output falls from 6,430 to 3,230 tokens here.
6: In an agent loop, when can the model think again?
Only before the first tool call
After each tool result, with interleaved thinking
Interleaved thinking lets the model reason about each observation; keep the thinking blocks in the history.

2: The agent wants to refund ₹25,000. What does the decide step do?
Calls issue_refund straight away
Returns a proposed plan for the next step to check
Proposing and acting are separate steps, so a check can sit between them.
3: The amount is above ₹10,000. What happens at interrupt()?
The run pauses, the state is saved under the thread id, and invoke returns
The process sleeps until someone answers
Nothing waits in memory; the saved state lets the run resume hours later, even on another server.
4: What should the reviewer see?
Just "Approve refund? yes or no"
The action, amount, reason and evidence
Reviewers can only judge what they are shown; a bare yes or no invites approval on autopilot.
5: On resume, the approve step runs again from its first line. What must be true of the code before interrupt()?
It must have no side effects, or be safe to repeat
Nothing: resumed steps skip earlier lines
LangGraph restarts the step on resume, so anything before the pause runs twice.
6: After approval the payment call times out and is retried. What stops a double refund?
The idempotency key tied to the ticket
Asking the reviewer to approve again
Approval decides whether to act; idempotency makes sure the action happens once.

2: Where should the agent’s code run?
In an isolated sandbox
In the app process, for speed
Model-written code must never share the host’s network, files or secrets.
3: The code tries to import requests. What should happen?
It fails: not on the allow-list
It runs: the model needs it
Only named imports are allowed.
4: Why cap steps and CPU time?
A loop that never ends stops instead of burning tokens and money
To make the model think faster
Limits bound cost and runaway behaviour.
5: The code raises an error. What next?
The traceback goes back to the model to fix
The task fails at once
Errors are observations the model can act on.
6: Can the code issue refunds?
Only through the same policy checks as any tool call
Yes, it is just Python
Code actions do not bypass action policies.

workflows: Workflows follow code paths you write in advance.
Split the task into fixed steps, each a model call.
Plain-code checks between steps stop bad input early.
A classifier sends each input down a specialised path.
Independent parts run in parallel; voting repeats a check.
Add agentic freedom only where fixed paths break.
react: The model reasons about what to do next.
It acts through a tool call with arguments.
The tool result is fed back as an observation.
It repeats until it can answer.
A hard step cap stops runaway loops.
growing history or errors as observations
Each call resends the history; errors come back as observations.
planexec: A planner writes the whole plan before acting.
Cheaper executors or plain tools run each step.
The planner is called again only when a step fails.
Plan once, so far fewer expensive calls.
ReWOO chains tools through variables such as #E1.
One final call writes the answer from the evidence.
reflect: A generator writes a first draft.
An evaluator checks it against clear criteria.
The generator revises and the loop repeats.
Feedback grounded in tests or rules is what makes it work.
cap rounds and keep the best
Cap the rounds and return the best draft.
search: Propose several thoughts at each step.
A value function scores each partial solution.
Keep only the best b candidates per level.
Prune impossible branches and back out of dead ends.
Use BFS, DFS or MCTS to explore the tree.
Calls grow with k, b and depth, so use it where mistakes commit you.
reasoning: The model reasons at length before it answers.
You set how much it may think with a budget or effort level.
More thinking helps on hard problems.
Thinking tokens are billed as output and add latency.
Easy requests get little or no thinking.
Gains flatten past a point, and the budget must fit the output limit.
hitl: The agent pauses before a risky or irreversible action.
a rule or limit in code
A rule in code decides which actions pause.
The run’s state is saved so it can wait.
a person approves, edits or rejects
A person approves, edits or rejects the action.
The run resumes from where it stopped.
The reviewer sees the evidence, and each decision is logged.
codeact: Each action is a short program.
Tools are called as functions from the code.
The code runs in a sandbox.

workflows: A health insurer’s claims emails fall into three types, each with a written procedure. The team is choosing between an autonomous agent and fixed code paths. What should it build first?
An autonomous agent with every claims tool
A router that sends each type down its own fixed chain
One long prompt listing all three procedures
A tree search over possible procedures
The steps are known in advance and the request types are few, so routing to fixed chains is cheaper, faster and easier to audit than an agent.
A bank’s router sends 4% of service requests to the wrong chain, and those customers get irrelevant replies. The misroutes are all low-confidence predictions. What is the most direct fix?
Add a confidence threshold with a general or human fallback
Replace the router with a larger model everywhere
Remove the router and use one prompt
Low-confidence predictions are where misroutes cluster, so a threshold that falls back to a general path or a human removes most of them.
A returns workflow extracts order details, then drafts a refund note. 6% of emails have no order number, and the drafts for them invent one. What stops this?
A plain-code gate that checks the order number before drafting
Asking the drafting prompt to be careful
A gate between chain steps is cheap and certain: stop and ask for the order number instead of letting a model guess.

One generic prompt costs ₹0.60 per claim. A router call costs ₹0.03; 70% of claims then take a 2-call small chain at ₹0.03 per call and 30% take the ₹0.60 prompt. What is the routed cost per 1,000 claims?
Router ₹30, small chains 700 × 2 × ₹0.03 = ₹42, large path 300 × ₹0.60 = ₹180. Total ₹252.
A hospital’s discharge workflow runs a medication check (3.0 s) and a summary (4.5 s) one after the other. Neither needs the other’s output. With sectioning, what is the latency of these two steps?
Run in parallel, the slower step sets the time: 4.5 s instead of 3.0 + 4.5 = 7.5 s.
Which of these are workflow patterns rather than agent behaviours? Select all that apply.
Prompt chaining with checks between steps
Routing each input to a specialised prompt
The model choosing which tool to call next from what it just saw
Running the same check three times and voting
Chaining, routing and parallelization (including voting) follow code paths you wrote. Choosing the next tool from an observation is agent behaviour.
A broker’s support desk sees 20 request types, but 3 of them make up 85% of volume and have fixed procedures. The rest are varied. What design fits?
Workflows for the top 3 types and an agent or human path for the rest
One workflow per request type, all 20
Fix the predictable bulk with workflows and send the varied tail to a more flexible path; building 20 rigid chains costs more than it saves.
A fraud check is voted on by three independent prompts, and a transaction is flagged when two agree. Each prompt costs ₹0.04. What does voting add per 1,000 transactions compared with one prompt?
Three prompts cost ₹0.12 against ₹0.04 for one, so voting adds ₹0.08 × 1,000 = ₹80.

A telecom’s workflow handles SIM, billing and roaming requests well, but open-ended complaints now make up 30% of traffic and 22% of all tasks end up misrouted. Which conclusions are reasonable? Select all that apply.
The fixed paths do not cover a large slice of the work
An agent or human path may be warranted for that slice
Adding voting to every chain will solve it
The router should be removed entirely
Unhandled tasks above about a fifth signal that fixed paths no longer fit; a more flexible path for that slice is the fix. Voting and removing the router do not address coverage.

A contract-review pipeline extracts clauses, classifies each and then summarises risks. A junior engineer wants to replace it with an agent “to make it smarter”. Accuracy and cost are already on target. What should the team do?
Replace it; agents are more capable
Keep the workflow and add an agent only for a measured gap
Add a tree search on top
Double the number of chain steps
Add agentic complexity only when it measurably helps. A workflow that meets its targets is cheaper and easier to audit.
A routing prompt classifies requests with probabilities. The code reads: if probs[route] > 0.7: route = "general". What is the effect?
Confident predictions go to the general path and unsure ones stay routed
Unsure predictions go to the general path
All requests go to the general path
The comparison is inverted: confident predictions fall back and unsure ones are routed. It should be < 0.7.
An EdTech platform grades essays with one call per essay. For high-stakes final exams it wants fewer grading errors and accepts higher cost. Which pattern fits?
Voting across several independent grading prompts
Voting runs the same task several times and aggregates, trading cost for fewer errors, which suits high-stakes decisions.
A shipment-exception workflow has a router with a 0.9 confidence threshold. Accuracy is high but costs doubled. Which are likely causes? Select all that apply.
Many confident-enough requests now fall back to the expensive general path
The threshold is set too high for this traffic
The gate between steps is too cheap
Sectioning is running steps in parallel
A very high threshold sends many routable requests to the general path, which costs more. Lowering it trades a little accuracy for large savings; gates and sectioning do not raise cost.
A lab-report workflow routes 60% of reports to a small-model chain at ₹0.10 and 40% to a large-model path at ₹0.50, plus a ₹0.02 router call on every report. What is the average cost per report?
A loan-application workflow calls a large model to check whether the PAN field is filled in. What is the best change?
Replace that step with a plain-code check
Use a larger model for more accuracy
Move it to the end of the chain
Only use a model where one is needed. A field-presence check is ordinary code: free, instant and exact.
A SaaS support team measures its new routed workflow. Which metrics tell it whether routing is working? Select all that apply.
Share of requests sent to the fallback path
Share of requests that fit no path and were misrouted
Per-route accuracy, fallback share and unhandled share show whether paths fit the traffic. Prompt length says nothing about quality.
A claims chain has three steps with success rates of 98%, 95% and 97%, and the steps fail independently. What share of claims pass all three?
0.98 × 0.95 × 0.97 = 0.9031, so about 90.3%. Chains multiply step error rates, which is why gates between steps matter.
Which case best justifies moving from a workflow to an agent?
Requests are few and well defined
The next action depends on what each lookup returns, and the paths cannot be listed in advance
Agents earn their cost when the path depends on observations nobody can predict. Fixed procedures, low latency and audit needs favour workflows.
A payments company splits a dispute summary into three independent sections (transaction facts, customer history, policy) and runs them in parallel. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
Latency is set by the slowest section
Total tokens stay roughly the same as running them one after another
Parallel sections must share one model call
Sectioning is a form of voting
Sectioning cuts latency to the slowest part while doing the same work, so tokens are similar. Each section is its own call, and voting is a different parallel pattern.
A router sends 55% of requests to path A (accuracy 96%), 30% to path B (92%) and 15% to a general path (80%). What is the overall accuracy?
react: A support agent diagnosing failed SIM swaps needs different checks depending on what each lookup returns. Which architecture fits?
A ReAct loop with a step cap
A single call with a large thinking budget
When the next step depends on the last observation, a ReAct loop fits; the cap keeps it bounded.
A ReAct agent keeps calling get_order with the same id until it hits the cap. Traces show the tool message contains the arguments, not the result. What is wrong?
The step cap is too low
The observation never reaches the model
The tool schema is too strict
If the tool result is not appended, the model never sees the outcome and repeats the call.
The system prompt and tools take 2,000 tokens, each step adds 800, and step n sends 2,000 + 800 × (n − 1) input tokens. How many input tokens do 6 steps send in total?
A tool that checks card status sometimes times out, and each timeout crashes the whole agent run. What change keeps runs alive?
Return the error to the model as a tool result
Returned as an observation, the error lets the model retry or choose another route instead of ending the run.
A broker’s order-investigation agent burns tokens on long traces. Which changes reduce tokens per task? Select all that apply.
Return only the fields the next step needs from each tool
Load only the tools relevant to the task
Raise the step cap from 8 to 20
Add more example traces to the system prompt
Compact results and fewer tool definitions shrink every call. A higher cap and longer prompts increase tokens.
With the OpenAI Agents SDK, what happens when an agent run exceeds max_turns?
The run silently returns the last message
The model is switched to a smaller one
The Runner raises MaxTurnsExceeded once the turn limit is passed, so you can stop gracefully or hand off.
A clinical-coding agent’s tool returns the full 6,000-token patient record on every lookup, and later calls get slow. Why do later calls suffer most?
Every later call resends all earlier tool results
ReAct history grows with each step, so a large early result is paid for again on every later call.
Which elements make up one ReAct step? Select all that apply.
A thought about what to do next
An action: a tool call with arguments
An observation: the tool result fed back
A fixed plan written before the task starts
ReAct interleaves thought, action and observation. A plan written up front is plan-and-execute.
A claims-status agent needs 5 model calls on a normal task and 6 when one tool retry happens. What is the smallest step cap that handles the retry case?
The cap must cover the calls the task needs, here 6 with a retry. Anything lower stops the run early.
Compared with 6 independent calls of 2,000 tokens each, how much more input does a 6-step ReAct loop send if each step adds 800 tokens of history?
Independent calls: 12,000. ReAct: 24,000 (see the growing history). The loop sends 12,000 more.
A ReAct agent loops on some tasks. Which safeguards belong in production? Select all that apply.
A hard step cap with a graceful hand-off
Logging every trace for replay and grading
Removing all error handling so failures are visible
Letting the model decide when the cap applies
Caps and traces keep loops bounded and debuggable. Crashing on errors and letting the model control the cap defeat the purpose.
A bank’s standard address-change process always runs the same four steps. A team built it as a ReAct agent and it costs three times its budget. What should they do?
Replace it with a fixed workflow
Re-deciding after every observation is wasted on a fixed procedure; a workflow runs the same steps far more cheaply.
Which smolagents class do its agents build on, as “an abstraction of ReAct framework”?
smolagents documents MultiStepAgent as the ReAct abstraction that its agents build on.
On ALFWorld and WebShop, how did ReAct compare with imitation and reinforcement learning baselines in the original paper?
It was 34 and 10 absolute points better
It was only tested on HotpotQA
The paper reports gains of 34 and 10 absolute points with only one or two in-context examples.
An EdTech tutor agent answers from a course-search tool. Which tool-result designs help the loop? Select all that apply.
Short results with the fields the model needs
Clear error messages that suggest a next step
Raw HTML pages of the course site
Identical wording for success and failure
Compact, informative results and helpful errors let the model decide well. Raw HTML bloats context and ambiguous results cause repeats.
A dispute agent makes 5 calls. Input per call is 1,200 tokens plus 220 tokens for each earlier step, and each call writes 100 output tokens. What is the total token count?
A ReAct agent sometimes answers after 3 steps even though the cap is 8. Is this a problem?
No: the cap is a limit, and it stopped because it had an answer
Yes: caps must equal the steps used
No: caps are ignored by the model
The loop ends when the model answers without a tool call. The cap only bounds runaway cases.
Why did ReAct reduce hallucination on HotpotQA and FEVER compared with reasoning alone?
It grounded reasoning in results from a Wikipedia API
Interleaving reasoning with lookups let the model check facts against retrieved results instead of inventing them.
A fleet-tracking agent has 25 tools loaded and often picks the wrong one. Which fixes are sensible? Select all that apply.
Load only the tools relevant to the task
Give tools distinct names and clear descriptions
Add more tools so the right one is always present
Fewer, clearly described tools make selection easier and shrink every call. Temperature and more tools make it worse.
A ReAct agent at a brokerage must never place trades without approval. Where should that control sit?
In code: the place_order tool requires an approval step before it runs
Safety-critical controls belong in code around the tool, not in instructions the model might ignore.
planexec: A rebooking task always needs the same five kinds of step, but choosing each step with a large model is slow and costly. Which architecture fits?
Plan-and-execute: plan once, execute cheaply, replan on failure
The steps are knowable in advance, so plan them once and run them with cheap executors.
ReAct makes 6 large-model calls of 3,000 tokens each. ReWOO makes a 1,500-token plan call and a 2,500-token solver call. What share of ReAct’s tokens does ReWOO use?
In ReWOO, what does a step input such as find_route(#E1) mean?
Call the model to rewrite the input
Fill #E1 with the stored result of step 1 and run the tool directly
Placeholders refer to earlier evidence, so tools chain without a model call in between.
A plan-and-execute loop reads: if result.ok: plan = replan(...). What goes wrong?
It replans after successes and never after failures
The condition is inverted. Replanning should happen when a step fails: if not result.ok.
Which are reported benefits of plan-and-execute over ReAct? Select all that apply.
Faster execution, since the large model is not consulted at every step
Lower cost, because smaller executors can run steps
Better results from planning the whole task up front
Better adaptation to surprising observations at every step
Speed, cost and whole-task planning are the claimed benefits. Step-by-step adaptation is ReAct’s strength, not plan-and-execute’s.
A 5-step plan-and-execute run makes one large planner call, five small executor calls and one large final call. How many large-model calls is that?
The planner and the final response are the only large calls: 2.
A plan assumed an item was in stock; step 2 shows it is not, but the executor carries on with steps 3 to 5. What is missing?
A replanning trigger when a result contradicts the plan
Replan when a step fails or the evidence contradicts the plan; otherwise a stale plan fails late.
LLMCompiler plans tool calls as a graph. What does that enable?
Every call uses the large model
A dependency graph lets independent calls run at the same time, cutting latency.
A hospital’s referral agent uses ReWOO. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
Tools run without a model call between them
A single solver call writes the final answer
The plan adapts automatically after every tool result
Every step needs a large-model executor
ReWOO plans once, fills placeholders from evidence and solves once. It does not adapt after each result unless you add replanning.
Plan-and-execute uses 2,500 tokens to plan, 5 executor calls of 1,200 tokens and a 2,000-token final call. What is the total?
A small, cheap model is used as the planner and writes plans that miss steps. What is the usual fix?
Use a small model for execution and a strong model for planning
Plan quality drives everything downstream, so plan with a strong model and save money on execution.
What did the ReWOO paper report on HotpotQA compared with a ReAct-style baseline?
About 5x token efficiency and about 4% higher accuracy
Twice the tokens for the same accuracy
ReWOO reported 5x token efficiency and a 4% accuracy gain on HotpotQA.
A plan-and-execute agent for shipment exceptions should replan when which of these happen? Select all that apply.
A step returns something the plan did not expect
A step finishes faster than expected
Replan on failures and surprises. Replanning after every success turns the design back into ReAct and loses the savings.
A research agent must pull four filings that do not depend on each other, then compare them. Which design minimises latency?
ReAct, one filing at a time
A planned graph that fetches all four in parallel, then one comparison call
Four separate agents talking to each other
Independent steps in a plan can run in parallel, as LLMCompiler does, followed by one join step.
With step 3 failing, ReAct takes 8 calls and 27,200 tokens. ReWOO with one replan uses 8,000 tokens. What share of ReAct’s tokens is that?
Plan-and-Solve prompting is best described as:
Asking the model to devise a plan and then carry it out, in one prompt
Plan-and-Solve is a prompting method: devise a plan, then solve step by step, all within one call.
Which checks make a planner’s output safer to execute? Select all that apply.
Require a structured list of steps with tool names
Validate each step’s tool name and arguments in code before running
Structured plans and code validation catch bad steps before they run. Free-form prose and skipped checks invite errors.
A course-scheduling agent’s plan uses #E2 = find_slots(#E1), but the tool for #E1 returned a list instead of a single id. What is the likely failure?
The placeholder is filled with a value of the wrong shape and the next tool breaks
Placeholders assume a result shape. Validate tool outputs before substitution, or replan when they differ.
Which scenario suits ReAct better than plan-and-execute?
An investigation where each lookup decides what to check next
When the next step cannot be known until the last result arrives, planning up front does not help.
A travel company moves from ReAct to plan-and-execute. Which should it measure to confirm the change helped? Select all that apply.
Task success rate, including failure cases
Number of tools registered with the planner
Calls, success and latency show whether the design is cheaper and still works. The tool count is not an outcome.
reflect: A coding agent’s generated functions fail tests about 30% of the time. The team has a full unit-test suite. Which loop fits best?
Evaluator–optimizer with the test results as feedback
Tests are exact external feedback, which is what makes an evaluator–optimizer loop reliable.
Asked to double-check its maths answers with no external tool, a model changes several correct answers to wrong ones. What does research suggest?
Without external feedback, models struggle to self-correct and can get worse
Self-critique only fails on long answers
Studies found LLMs struggle to self-correct reasoning without external feedback, and performance can drop.
Generation costs ₹1.50 and evaluation ₹0.40, every draft is evaluated, and 50% pass on draft 1, 30% after one revision and 20% after two. What is the average cost per letter?
A clause-revision loop tracks the best draft but ends with return draft. Round 4 scored lower than round 3. What is shipped?
Returning the last draft ships the regression. Return the best-scoring draft instead.
Which make a good evaluator for a policy-wording loop? Select all that apply.
A rules table checked in code
The generator’s own opinion with no criteria
Checkable, external criteria give specific feedback. Vague instructions and unguided self-opinion do not.
Reflexion stores written lessons from failed attempts and reuses them on later attempts
Self-Refine revises within one attempt; Reflexion keeps verbal lessons in memory across attempts.
A product-description loop has no round cap, and some items go through 12 rounds for tiny gains. What is the fix?
Cap the rounds and stop when the criteria pass
Cap rounds and stop on pass; unbounded loops burn tokens on marginal gains.
Reflexion reported what pass@1 on HumanEval, against 80% for GPT-4 at the time?
Reflexion reached 91% pass@1 on HumanEval using test feedback.
A loan-letter loop improves from 62 to 92 in three rounds with rules feedback. Which choices would lower cost without losing quality? Select all that apply.
Store lessons from earlier letters so first drafts start higher
Stop as soon as every check passes
Memory raises first drafts and early stopping avoids extra rounds. Self-critique lowers quality and removing the cap raises cost.
A critique says “the clause could be clearer”. The revision barely changes. What would help most?
A critique that lists the specific failed rules and why
Specific failures tell the generator exactly what to fix; vague critique produces vague revisions.
When does Anthropic suggest the evaluator–optimizer workflow fits?
When there are clear evaluation criteria and iterative refinement adds measurable value
Evaluator–optimizer suits tasks with clear criteria where feedback measurably improves the output.
Self-Refine reported roughly what average improvement across seven tasks, without training?
Self-Refine reported about a 20% absolute average improvement across seven tasks.
A dispute-reply loop scores drafts 70, 82, 79, 85 over four rounds. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
The loop should return the round 4 draft, the best
The loop should return the round 3 draft
Round 3 fell from 82 to 79, a regression; the best overall is round 4 at 85, which is also the last here.
A grading loop uses an LLM judge that has never been checked against human graders. What is the main risk?
The loop optimises towards a miscalibrated judge
An uncalibrated judge steers revisions in the wrong direction. Calibrate the evaluator before trusting it.
Each round costs ₹1.60 and memory adds a one-off ₹0.05. With memory, a letter reaches its target in 2 rounds; without, in 3. What is saved per 1,000 letters with memory?
Which task gains least from a reflection loop?
Policy letters checked against a rules table
A creative slogan with no agreed criteria
SQL queries checked by running them on a test database
With no clear criteria, the evaluator has nothing reliable to check, so revisions add cost without dependable gains.
A reflection loop for SQL generation should include which of these? Select all that apply.
